clinicalPearls: A rare recessive defect of glutathione synthesis producing an oxidant-sensitive chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia
The enzyme catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of glutathione production, so deficiency depletes red-cell glutathione
Low glutathione leaves the red cell poorly protected against oxidant stress, and haemolysis may worsen with oxidant drugs or infection
Some patients have neurological features such as spinocerebellar degeneration and peripheral neuropathy, reflecting glutathione depletion in other tissues
The anaemia is Coombs-negative and the film may show non-specific oxidative changes
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating low red-cell glutathione, reduced enzyme activity and a GCLC mutation
Management is supportive with folate and transfusion when needed, and above all avoidance of oxidant drugs and foods known to precipitate haemolysis
reference.pathophysiology: Gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase, also called glutamate-cysteine ligase, catalyses the first and rate-limiting step in the synthesis of glutathione, the tripeptide that defends the red cell against oxidative injury. Deficiency lowers red-cell glutathione, leaving haemoglobin and membrane proteins vulnerable to oxidant damage; the resulting chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia is characteristically exacerbated by oxidant stress from certain drugs or infections. Because glutathione is important throughout the body, severe deficiency can also cause neurological dysfunction.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film for oxidative changes
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Molecular testing of the GCLC gene
redFlags: Acute haemolytic crisis triggered by oxidant drug exposure or infection
Progressive neurological deterioration in severe deficiency
Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection
reference.prognosis: The haemolytic anaemia is usually chronic and manageable if oxidant triggers are avoided; prognosis is worse when significant neurological involvement is present.
pitfalls: Failing to advise strict avoidance of oxidant drugs and foods
Confusing the disorder with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency without measuring glutathione
Overlooking neurological signs that indicate systemic glutathione depletion
Neglecting iron-overload monitoring in transfused patients
management: Avoidance of oxidant triggers, including oxidant drugs and where relevant foods, with prompt treatment of infections that precipitate haemolysis
Supportive care of the chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with folic acid supplementation and red-cell transfusion during severe crises
Consideration of antioxidant supplementation such as vitamin E as an adjunct
Monitoring of haemolysis with blood count, reticulocytes, bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, and of iron status in transfused patients
Neurological assessment and supportive management where spinocerebellar degeneration or peripheral neuropathy is present
Genetic counselling for this recessive disorder with GCLC molecular confirmation and family testing
Multidisciplinary input from haematology and clinical genetics
